prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat bands in twisted bilayer graphene at a magic angle and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states, opening the field of moire quantum materials.

statement.case_for: I keep magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B013) with Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero. After reading all eight statements I find that no member disputes the facts on which my case rests: the 2011 continuum-model prediction of flat bands at a magic angle, the 2018 observation of correlated insulators and gate-tunable superconducting domes, and their reproduction by many groups across transport, scanning-probe and optical methods and across several moire platforms. What is new is not a single device but a controllable many-body platform in which one geometric parameter tunes the ratio of interaction to bandwidth. That is the kind of conceptual step I weigh most heavily. The citation I propose asserts only what is secure (flat bands, correlated insulating and superconducting states) and says nothing about the pairing mechanism, which addresses the maturity objection raised by Johansson, Danielsson, Kroll, Lindroth and Pearce. The theory-experiment structure also gives a natural three-person credit with a visible logic: two for the prediction, one for the discovery.
statement.case_against: The round-1 exchange has strengthened the objections. First, six of eight members place B001 first, with an identical two-name credit that raises no allocation problem, whereas the B013 credit forces an exclusion that Andrei's early STM and transport evidence makes hard to defend on priority alone. I still judge the exclusion defensible, because her work preceded the magic-angle prediction and did not reveal the correlated or superconducting states, but I concede it will be contested publicly. Second, the field is eight years old, the pairing mechanism is open, and twist-angle disorder makes device-level reproducibility uneven, so the committee carries more interpretive risk than with a clock whose accuracy is checked clock against clock. Third, Bistritzer and Jarillo-Herrero were early in their careers when the work was done, and MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero were not the only contributors to the experimental programme. If the committee prefers maturity and clean attribution over conceptual novelty, B001 is the better choice and I would vote for it without reluctance.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that a platform whose central question (the origin of the superconductivity) is unresolved is a weaker case than a measurement whose accuracy is directly demonstrated, and that the clock needs no committee judgment on contested credit.
responses.response: The asymmetry you describe is real, but it concerns the follow-up questions and not what the prize would honour. The question of what was discovered is settled for B013: flat bands at a magic angle, correlated insulators and superconducting domes, reproduced widely. A prize for the mechanism of the superconductivity would be premature and I would not support one. I do accept your credit point more than I did in round 1: the clock has the cleaner attribution and I cannot claim B013 does. Your offer to support B013 as a second choice is noted. Where we still differ is on how much weight the Andrei exclusion should carry; I treat it as a cost to be stated openly, not as a reason to wait.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, says the superconductivity is contested and device-level reproducibility is uneven, so the maturity concern applies more strongly to B013 than to B001, and that Andrei's STM work remains an unresolved allocation problem.
responses.response: I accept that reproducibility is uneven at the level of individual devices and phase-diagram details; that is why my citation names only the flat-band prediction and the existence of correlated insulating and superconducting states. Those two features have been seen in many laboratories and platforms, including twisted double bilayers and transition-metal dichalcogenide moire systems, so the discovery does not depend on one sample type. On Andrei, I still do not see a Pearce-style substitution for Bistritzer as defensible: he co-wrote the continuum model with MacDonald and the continuum model is what predicted the magic angle. Her evidence concerned van Hove singularities and velocity renormalisation at earlier stages. I maintain that the exclusion should be stated explicitly in our rationale, and I recognise that you and others will weigh it more heavily than I do.

responses.point: Eriksson holds B013 first on the same trio, treats the Andrei question as the hard allocation choice, and notes that the pairing mechanism should not enter the citation and that metrology is outside his expertise.
responses.response: We agree on the trio and on the wording. I would add two things to the discussion of your caution about the 2010 graphene and 2016 topological-phases prizes. The 2010 prize rewarded isolation and properties of a single layer, and the 2016 prize rewarded topological phase transitions; neither concerned twist-controlled flat bands and interaction-driven phases, so I do not count the overlap against B013 any more than I count the 2005 and 2012 overlap against B001. I also share your deference on metrology: my own judgement of the clock case rests on how Danielsson, Kroll and Lindroth describe it, and I should not let that deference become a reason to rank it first without testing it.

responses.point: Danielsson argues that the lattice clock's distinct idea is many-atom interrogation at a magic wavelength, giving statistical gain and different systematics, and that the pending redefinition of the second is a reason to act, not to wait.
responses.response: This is a persuasive answer to the question the chair raised and it moves me. I had read the lattice clock mainly as a refinement of optical frequency metrology after 2005 and 2012. The point that state-insensitive trapping of thousands of neutral atoms changes the stability limit and the class of systematic effects makes the clock a distinct step and not a repeat of the ion-clock prize, and I withdraw some of my earlier weight on the overlap argument. I also agree that the redefinition of the second should not be a precondition. What I still weigh differently is the conceptual breadth: a clock is a very good instrument, whereas moire materials opened a new set of phases to study.

responses.point: Kroll says B001 is not merely incremental because a different solution to the stability problem was found, and that Katori, rather than any later group, should anchor the citation, while accepting the early-credit question is not fully settled.
responses.response: Your stated priority of Katori as anchor for the citation seems right to me, and so does your caveat that you and others have not independently verified the chronology for Lemonde, Ido, Takamoto and the PTB, NIST and Paris groups. I have no more reliable knowledge of that chronology than you do, so I cannot resolve that uncertainty either. It matters for the comparison: both B001 and B013 exclude people with real claims, and B001's exclusions are less visible to me only because the history is less familiar. I would therefore not count the allocation problem as a decisive asymmetry between the two.

responses.point: Johansson would revisit B013 if the correlated-insulator physics were argued to be settled enough, and sees the Andrei question as more than an allocation detail because her STM evidence predates the transport discovery.
responses.response: The correlated insulators and superconducting domes are settled as phenomena in the sense that matters for a prize: they have been reproduced in many laboratories and platforms and the observation does not depend on a particular model of the pairing. What is not settled is the mechanism and the full phase diagram, and I would not claim otherwise. On Andrei I accept that a three-person limit forces a choice and that her evidence predates the transport discovery. But the transport discovery is also what the magic-angle prediction pointed to, and the prize would rest on prediction plus discovery together. I do not expect this to move you, but I hope the exclusion is at least judged on that logic.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept the exclusion of Eva Andrei as defensible when stated openly, or whether it makes the B013 credit too contestable to award this year.
Whether the magic-angle field has matured enough, given the unresolved pairing mechanism and uneven device-level reproducibility, to be preferred over a clock with settled interpretation.
The priority chronology among Katori, Ye and other early lattice-clock groups, which I have not been able to verify and which affects how clean the B001 credit really is.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict has arisen from the discussion and none is apparent from my profile for B013, B001 or B024. My documented co-authors and institutions (Fulde, Gustavsson, Wilkinson, Einarsson, Candelier, Pumir, Meibohm; Max Planck, Oxford, Freiburg, Gothenburg) do not include any credited candidate. I noted that my own research is in statistical physics and neural networks, not condensed-matter experiment or precision metrology, so my judgement on both leading candidates relies on the arguments of colleagues.
